Week of May 03, 2026

Okay so the funniest thing happened this week. Shawn Baker dropped a video called "Why Everyone's Leaving Carnivore" and then 1,400 commenters showed up to say they're absolutely not leaving. An 83-year-old who's been eating this way for six years. A 74-year-old who reversed AFIB, psoriasis, and diverticulitis and says he's "in for the duration." Someone who dropped 70 lbs in six months with arthritis gone. The comments read less like a quitting post and more like a carnivore hall of fame. If you've been wondering about the dropout rate yourself, Sarah actually broke down why most people quit in week three and what actually gets them through it.

Meanwhile, HomeSteadHow shared three years of carnivore lessons in ten minutes, and the comment section turned into its own masterclass. People talking about fasting, skin improvements, autoimmune relief, losing 100+ pounds on the lion diet. The lesson that kept coming up? Fasting and carnivore go together better than most people expect. Over on Reddit, someone posted their very first day jumping in, got the whole community cheering them on with tips like "add more fat" and "don't overthink it." And a 13-month post from r/carnivorediet hit different this week, with the author saying carnivore now feels completely natural, like they've always eaten this way. "Getting out of fat prison" was their phrase, and honestly that landed.

The budget conversation is getting loud too. Steak and Butter Gal's cheap ground beef meal plan is pulling serious numbers, and the comments have people inventing skillet meatloaves with pork rinds and sharing what five meals a week actually looks like at scale. The community is clearly figuring out how to eat this way without spending like it's a steakhouse every night. So here's what I want to know: what's your go-to cheap carnivore meal that you actually look forward to eating every single week?

key_insights:
# Marcus's Weekly Carnivore Content Analysis

## What the Numbers Say

Shawn Baker's "Why Everyone's Leaving Carnivore" pulled 138,101 views and 1,434 comments in under a week. The comments tell the real story: people aren't leaving. They're reversing AFIB, clearing psoriasis, staying at 83 years old with zero plans to quit. The headline is bait. The audience called it out and kept scrolling. HomeSteadHow delivered 108,958 views with a simple value proposition: three years of lessons in ten minutes. The top insight in comments? Carnivore plus fasting is the actual protocol. Budget content is also moving. Steak and Butter Gal's cheap meal plan hit 48,098 views with a 7.7% like rate. That's strong signal.

## This Week's Signal

Three themes are driving engagement right now. First, retention and longevity. The community is pushing back hard on "carnivore is dying" narratives. Long-term results (6 years, 13 months, 2 months) are getting 161 to 291 upvotes on Reddit. People want proof it works long-term, and the community is delivering it. Second, budget optimization. 48k views on a cheap meal plan confirms the cost barrier is real and the audience wants solutions. Third, controversy converts. Kent Carnivore's Packham video hit 771 comments on 50,408 views. That's a 1.5% comment rate, well above average. Outrage around animal welfare and hypocrisy drives conversation.

## The Opportunity

Write the budget protocol post. The view counts and like rates on budget carnivore content are not a coincidence. Give readers a concrete cost-per-day number, a shopping list, and a weekly meal structure. The cholesterol myth angle (Dr. Westman, 15,744 views) is evergreen and keeps surfacing. A post pairing long-term carnivore results with the latest cholesterol data would land right now. Reddit's transformation content ("getting out of fat prison," 268 upvotes) signals that before-and-after framing with real timelines is what the audience shares. Build content around measurable outcomes and specific durations, not vague promises.

qa_section.question: Why do people quit carnivore even when it's working for them?
qa_section.answer: It's a fair question, and the honest answer is that adherence on any restrictive diet is complicated. The research on long-term dietary adherence consistently shows that social pressure, food environment, and cost are bigger barriers than biology. On carnivore specifically, the three things I see most often are: the social friction of eating differently at restaurants and family dinners, the cost of quality meat, and what I'd call the 'I'm fixed now' mistake where people feel so good they think they can go back to old habits. What the comment sections on videos like Shawn Baker's recent one make clear is that the people who stay are almost always the ones who connected carnivore to resolving a real health problem, whether that's autoimmune disease, gut issues, or metabolic dysfunction. When the stakes are personal, people stay. When it's just a weight loss experiment, they drift. Your situation might be different, but if you're struggling with adherence, it's worth asking whether you've given it long enough to see the result that would actually matter to you.

qa_section.question: I keep getting leg cramps and poor sleep on carnivore. What's actually going on?
qa_section.answer: This is one of the most common things I hear from people in weeks two through six of carnivore, and the good news is it's almost always fixable. When you remove carbohydrates, your kidneys excrete significantly more sodium, and that shift cascades into how your body handles potassium and magnesium too. The sodium-potassium pump, which regulates muscle contraction and nerve signaling, runs on these electrolytes, and when sodium drops, the whole system gets dysregulated. That's your leg cramps. The sleep connection is real too: sodium helps regulate aldosterone and cortisol, and low sodium at night can spike cortisol in ways that fragment sleep. The fix that works for most people is consistent sodium throughout the day, not just at meals. Some people do well with a pinch of sea salt in water mid-morning and mid-afternoon. The research shows that sodium needs can jump from the standard 2,300 mg daily recommendation to 3,000 to 5,000 mg on a very low carbohydrate diet. Start there before reaching for anything more complicated.

qa_section.question: What are the cheapest high-quality protein sources for carnivore when beef is expensive?
qa_section.answer: This one comes up constantly, and it's a legitimate concern. Quality meat is not cheap right now. Here's what I've seen work for people watching their budget. Eggs are still the best value in protein. Cost per gram of complete protein, nothing touches them. Ground beef, especially when bought in bulk or family packs, is typically cheaper per pound than steaks and has similar nutritional density. Chicken thighs with skin are underrated on carnivore. They've got a better fat profile than breasts and usually cost half as much. Canned sardines and mackerel are genuinely excellent, high in omega-3s, loaded with selenium and vitamin D, and inexpensive. Chicken livers are almost free by comparison to muscle meat and have an extraordinary nutrient density, including preformed vitamin A, B12, folate, and iron. You don't need ribeye every day to do this well. A budget carnivore plate of eggs, ground beef, and sardines hits most of your nutritional targets. The research on nutrient adequacy on carnivore diets generally shows the main variables are organ meat inclusion and fat-to-protein ratio, not the specific cuts you choose.
